title: INFWAD – Oefentoets 2: HTML, CSS, JavaScript & TypeScript
description: The HTML, CSS, JavaScript and TypeScript questions from the second practice exam (13 questions). The React and ASP.NET Core questions are left out.

questions.title: CSS – Specificity
questions.explanation: A declaration with `!important` wins over all normal declarations, even over an id selector and an inline `style` attribute. So `color: blue !important` wins.

questions.title: HTML – Headings
questions.text: What is the correct element for the most important text heading?
questions.explanation: `<h1>` is the most important heading and `<h6>` the least important. `<header>` is a section container and `<head>` holds metadata, not visible content.

questions.title: CSS – Selectors
questions.text: Which CSS selector is correct for targeting an element with `class="header"`?
questions.explanation: A dot selects by class (`.header`), a hash selects by id (`#header`). `@` starts an at-rule such as `@media`.

questions.title: HTML & CSS – Semantics
questions.text: Why is it important to use semantic names with HTML and CSS?
questions.explanation: Semantic elements and class names help screen readers, search engines and developers, and make later changes less error-prone. All the statements are true.

options.text: It lowers the risk of mistakes when changing code later
It makes the code easier to read for developers

questions.title: JavaScript – The DOM
questions.explanation: The DOM is a browser API (a W3C/WHATWG standard), not part of the JavaScript language. It is a tree of nodes, including text and comment nodes, and you can change it at any time after the page loads.

options.text: The DOM is part of the JavaScript language specification.
The DOM cannot be modified once the page is loaded.
The DOM is an API that represents the document as a node tree and is independent of JavaScript.
The DOM only contains element nodes, not text or comment nodes.

questions.title: JavaScript – The DOM
questions.text: Which method is used to create a new HTML element using JavaScript?
questions.explanation: `document.createElement('input')` creates the element; you then add it to the page with e.g. `appendChild` or `append`. The other methods do not exist.

questions.title: TypeScript – Arrays
questions.explanation: `map` turns every element into something new, so `map(x => x.name)` gives an array of names. `map` and `reduce` need a function, not `name`, and `filter` only keeps or drops elements (it would return the user objects).

questions.title: TypeScript – Block scope
questions.explanation: `let` is block-scoped: the inner `x` only exists inside `{ }` and shadows the outer one there. After the block, the outer `x` (1) is used again.

questions.title: JavaScript – Asynchronous code
questions.text: What is the main reason JavaScript can handle asynchronous tasks despite being single-threaded?
questions.explanation: Web APIs (timers, fetch, events) do the waiting outside the JavaScript thread. When they finish, their callbacks go into a queue, and the event loop runs them once the call stack is empty.

options.text: It secretly spawns multiple JavaScript threads
The JavaScript engine uses the Event Loop to coordinate tasks handled by Web APIs
All asynchronous tasks are executed in parallel on the CPU
JavaScript pauses synchronous code until asynchronous tasks finish

questions.title: JavaScript – Event loop
questions.text:
```js
console.log("A")

setTimeout(() => console.log("B"), 10)

console.log("C")
```

What is the correct console.log output order for the JavaScript code above?
questions.explanation: All synchronous code runs first (A, then C). The `setTimeout` callback is only run by the event loop after the timer is done and the call stack is empty, so B comes last.

questions.title: TypeScript – Generics
questions.explanation: The array is not empty and has no `undefined` values, so `fn` (x + 1) is applied to every element, like `map`. The result is `{ status: 'OK', result: [2, 3, 4] }`, so `[2, 3, 4]` is logged.
